pos: adv. (in a just manner; according to what is right; of judgment, of rule, and of the Christian life)
etymology: Old English rihtwis, right-wise, with the adverbial ending. The Hebrew tsedeq and the Greek dikaios both carry the sense of conformity to a standard outside the actor.
biblical_def: The word governs three things in Scripture. First, the bench: Moses charged the judges, “Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him” (Deu 1:16) — and the stranger is named deliberately, so that no man is judged by whether he belongs. Lemuel's mother charges a king in the same terms: “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9). Second, the throne of God: the nations are called to be glad and sing for joy “for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth” (Psa 67:4), and the missionary psalm says among the heathen that the LORD reigneth, “he shall judge the people righteously” (Psa 96:10). That God judges is presented as news the nations should be glad to hear, because a world with an unrighteous judge or no judge at all is a worse world. Third, the life: the grace of God that bringeth salvation teaches us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world. Righteous living is not what earns the grace; it is what the grace teaches.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines righteously as in a righteous manner; honestly; uprightly; equitably; without injustice or partiality.
webster_full: RIGHTEOUSLY, adv. In a righteous manner; honestly; uprightly; equitably.
2. Without injustice or crime.
He shall judge the people righteously. Ps. xcvi.
scriptures: Deu 1:16
And I charged your judges at that time, saying, Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him.
Say among the heathen that the LORD reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved: he shall judge the people righteously.
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
corruption_summary: Justice is now expected to weigh the parties rather than the case, so that the identity of the litigant is treated as evidence — which is precisely the partiality the law forbids in both directions.
corruption_paragraphs: The Mosaic law states the standard twice and in both directions, which is the detail most often missed. Leviticus 19:15: ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour. It is obvious enough why a judge must not favour the mighty — that is the classic corruption of courts, and the prophets thunder against it. What startles the modern reader is the first clause: the judge may not favour the poor man either. Exodus 23:3 repeats it, neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause. The reason is that righteous judgment is judgment of a cause, and the moment a litigant's class, wealth, or group becomes evidence, the cause has stopped being tried. Contemporary theories of justice increasingly do exactly this in a new idiom, treating the identity of the parties as determinative of the merits, and Christians sometimes adopt the framework because its stated concern for the oppressed sounds biblical. The concern is biblical; the method is the one Leviticus forbids. Scripture's own remedy for the poor man is not a thumb on the scale but a set of positive duties — gleaning, the year of release, the prohibition on usury, the command to plead his cause — and then a court that hears him exactly as it hears everyone else. Deuteronomy 1:16 puts the stranger in the sentence for that reason.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsedeq (H6664), rightness, justice; mishpat (H4941), judgment, a legal decision; Greek dikaios (G1342), righteous, and its adverb, conforming to the standard.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — rightness, what conforms to the standard; judge righteously, and the LORD our righteousness; Deuteronomy 1:16, Jeremiah 23:6.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, a legal decision, the due of a case; paired constantly with tsedeq as the two pillars of God's throne; Psalm 89:14, Amos 5:24.
Greek dikaios (G1342) — righteous, just; the adverb in Titus 2:12 and of Christ committing Himself to him that judgeth righteously; 1 Peter 2:23.
usage: “Judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him” — the stranger named on purpose.
“He shall judge the people righteously” — the news the nations are told to be glad about.
“Live soberly, righteously, and godly” — what grace teaches, not what earns it.

pos: adv. (with fidelity; honestly; in a manner that may be trusted without supervision)
etymology: From faith, Latin fides, trust, with the adverbial ending. In the Authorized Version it is very often used of handling other people's money.
biblical_def: Scripture's clearest picture of faithfulness is an audit that was not performed. When Jehoash repaired the house of the LORD, “they reckoned not with the men, into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen: for they dealt faithfully” (2Ki 12:15). The same thing is said, in almost the same words, of Josiah's repairs a century and a half later: “there was no reckoning made with them of the money that was delivered into their hand, because they dealt faithfully” (2Ki 22:7). Two kings, two building funds, and in both cases the accounting was waived because the character of the men was known. Jehoshaphat used the word when he set judges in the land: “Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart” (2Ch 19:9). Hezekiah's reform produced the same result at the storehouses: they “brought in the offerings and the tithes and the dedicated things faithfully” (2Ch 31:12). Faithfulness in these passages is not intensity or zeal. It is the settled reliability of a man whose conduct is the same whether or not anyone is counting — and Paul says it is the one thing required in a steward.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faithfully as in a faithful manner; with good faith; sincerely; honestly; with strict adherence to allegiance and duty.
webster_full: FAITHFULLY, adv. In a faithful manner; with good faith.
2. With strict adherence to allegiance and duty; as, a soldier serves his country faithfully.
3. With strict observance of promises, vows, covenants or duties; without failure of performance; honestly.
scriptures: Moreover they reckoned not with the men, into whose hand they delivered the money to be bestowed on workmen: for they dealt faithfully.
And he charged them, saying, Thus shall ye do in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
corruption_summary: Ministry and public life are now measured by visible outcome, and the biblical measure — whether the man could be trusted without an audit — has almost no place in the assessment.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Kings 12:15 is a startling sentence for a modern reader: they made no reckoning with the men who handled the temple money, because they dealt faithfully. No receipts, no committee, no external audit. The dictionary does not read this as advice to abolish financial controls — Paul himself took pains in the matter of the collection, providing for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men, and travelling with delegates chosen by the churches. What the verse establishes is the standard by which a man was judged: not what he produced, but whether he could be trusted where no one was looking. That standard has largely dropped out of contemporary assessment. Ministries are weighed by attendance, giving, reach, and growth; leaders are promoted on results; and the question of whether a man is faithful in that which is least is treated as a private matter that will presumably sort itself out. It does not sort itself out, as the steady record of ministry collapse shows — and the collapses are almost never failures of ability. Christ makes faithfulness in the least the diagnostic of faithfulness in much (Luk 16:10). Paul reduces the whole requirement for a steward to one word: it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful. And the commendation the Lord gives at the end is not Well done, thou successful servant.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'emunah (H530), firmness, fidelity, steadiness; 'aman (H539), to be firm, to trust, whence amen; Greek pistos (G4103), faithful, trustworthy.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'emunah (H530) — firmness, steadiness, faithfulness; the workmen who needed no reckoning, and the just who shall live by his faith; 2 Kings 12:15, Habakkuk 2:4.
Hebrew 'aman (H539) — to be firm, to support, to trust; the root of amen, and of Abraham believing God; Genesis 15:6, Isaiah 7:9.
Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy, believing; required in stewards, and said of God who calleth you; 1 Corinthians 4:2, 1 Thessalonians 5:24.
usage: “They reckoned not with the men…for they dealt faithfully” — an audit waived on character.
“In the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart” — Jehoshaphat's charge to judges.
“He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” — the diagnostic.

pos: adv. (with favour freely given; in a manner that bestows what is not earned)
etymology: Latin gratia, favour, from gratus, pleasing. The Hebrew chanan means to bend or stoop toward in kindness — the posture of a superior toward one who has no claim.
biblical_def: Jacob, meeting Esau after twenty years and fearing for his life, twice uses the word of God. Of his children: “The children which God hath graciously given thy servant” (Gen 33:5). Of his estate: “Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough” (Gen 33:11). The man who had schemed for a birthright and cheated for a blessing now says plainly that everything he has was given, and that he has enough. The psalmist asks for grace in the matter of the law itself: “Remove from me the way of lying: and grant me thy law graciously” (Psa 119:29) — even obedience must be given, not achieved. And Hosea puts the word in the mouth of a returning people: “Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips” (Hos 14:2). They come with nothing but words, ask to be received on the ground of grace alone, and the next verses record what God says in reply: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines graciously as kindly; with kind condescension; in a friendly manner; also, favourably, with kindness and mercy.
webster_full: GRACIOUSLY, adv. Kindly; with kind condescension.
He graciously received the petition.
2. In a pleasing manner. 3. Fortunately; luckily; favorably.
scriptures: Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee; because God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough. And he urged him, and he took it.
Remove from me the way of lying: and grant me thy law graciously.
Hos 14:2
Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.
corruption_summary: Grace is widely preached as God's indulgence toward sin rather than His free favour toward the guilty, which is a different thing entirely and produces a different Christian.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 14:2 is a model prayer for a nation that has nothing left to offer: take with you words, and turn to the LORD; say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously. Two requests, in that order. Take away the iniquity — not overlook it, not reclassify it, take it away. And then receive us on the ground of Your free favour, since there is no other ground. The modern corruption of grace collapses the two requests into one and drops the first. Grace becomes a divine disposition to be relaxed about sin, a permanent amnesty that makes repentance unnecessary and sanctification optional, and its practical slogan is that God accepts you as you are — which is true about the terms of admission and false about the terms of continuance, since He does not intend to leave anyone as they are. Paul faced the same error and answered it with a question and an argument: shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein? Titus 2:11-12 gives the positive statement, and it is the plainest verse on the subject: the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly. Grace is a teacher, not an indulgence. And Jacob's two sentences show what it produces in a man: everything I have was given, and I have enough.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanan (H2603), to bend or stoop in kindness, to show favour; chen (H2580), grace, favour; Greek charis (G5485), grace, unmerited favour.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to stoop in kindness toward an inferior, to be gracious; the LORD's own self-description, and the Aaronic blessing; Exodus 33:19, Numbers 6:25.
Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour, acceptance; Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD; Genesis 6:8, Proverbs 3:34.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, free favour; by grace are ye saved through faith, and the grace that teaches; Ephesians 2:8, Titus 2:11-12.
usage: “God hath dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough” — the supplanter's settled account.
“Grant me thy law graciously” — even obedience is asked for as a gift.
“Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously” — two requests, in that order.

pos: adv. (with patience; enduring without murmuring; waiting without fretting)
etymology: Latin patiens, suffering, bearing, from pati, to suffer. Patience in Scripture is not placidity of temperament but endurance under a weight.
biblical_def: David's two great patience texts sit in adjacent psalms and give the two halves of the grace. Psalm 37: “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass” (Psa 37:7) — patience defined against a specific irritant, the visible success of a wicked man. Psalm 40 gives the outcome: “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry” (Psa 40:1), and what follows is the horrible pit, the miry clay, the rock, the new song. Paul asks Agrippa to hear him patiently (Act 26:3), the courtesy of a prisoner who has one hearing and needs it not to be cut short. And Hebrews gives the pattern case: “after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise” (Heb 6:15) — Abraham, twenty-five years between the promise of a son and Isaac's birth, and the whole argument of the passage is that God swore by Himself because He could swear by no greater, so that we might have strong consolation. Patience in Scripture is therefore never passive resignation. It is active waiting on a God who has bound Himself by an oath.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines patiently as with calmness or composure; without discontent or murmuring; without repining; with the temper that endures evils.
webster_full: PATIENTLY, adv. With calmness or composure; without discontent or murmuring.
2. Without vexation or discontent; without haste.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
scriptures: Psa 37:7
Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.
Psa 40:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.
Heb 6:15
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
corruption_summary: Psalm 37 is the answer to a question the age asks constantly — why the wicked prosper — and it answers not with an explanation but with a command not to fret and a horizon of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 37 opens by naming the exact temptation: fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. It repeats the command three times in the first eight verses, and it never once explains why God permits their prosperity. Instead it changes the time horizon: for they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb. Asaph works the same problem in Psalm 73 and describes the collapse it nearly caused in him — my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped — and the turn comes not from an argument but from a place: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. Our age poses the prosperity of the wicked as a philosophical objection to God's existence, and Christians frequently try to answer it as though it were one. Scripture treats it as a temptation to envy, and prescribes accordingly: rest, wait, fret not, delight thyself also in the LORD, commit thy way unto him. The patience commanded is not an agreement to stop caring about injustice — the same psalm promises that the meek shall inherit the earth and that the LORD laughs at the wicked, for he seeth that his day is coming. It is a refusal to settle accounts on a timescale shorter than God's. Abraham waited twenty-five years and obtained the promise; the psalmist waited and got a rock under his feet and a new song in his mouth.
roots_summary: Hebrew chuwl (H2342), to wait, to writhe in waiting; qavah (H6960), to wait, to look eagerly for; Greek makrothumeo (G3114), to be long-tempered, to endure patiently.
roots_lines: Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to wait, and also to writhe or travail; the waiting of Psalm 37:7 is not comfortable; Psalm 37:7.
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; Psalm 40:1, Isaiah 40:31.
Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be long-tempered, to bear long; Abraham patiently enduring, and the husbandman waiting for the precious fruit of the earth; Hebrews 6:15, James 5:7.
usage: “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself” — patience defined against a specific irritant.
“I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me” — and a new song followed.
“After he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise” — twenty-five years, and an oath behind it.

pos: adv. (without knowledge; unwittingly; of sin committed in ignorance and of worship offered blindly)
etymology: Latin ignorare, not to know. Scripture uses the word in a technical legal sense — the unwitting act — and in a spiritual sense for sincere worship of an unknown God.
biblical_def: The law makes express provision for the unwitting sin: “the priest shall make an atonement for the soul that sinneth ignorantly, when he sinneth by ignorance before the LORD, to make an atonement for him; and it shall be forgiven him” (Num 15:28). Ignorance reduces neither the reality of the sin nor the need of a sacrifice; it changes the remedy from execution to atonement. The same principle governs the manslayer: “Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past” may flee to a city of refuge (Deu 19:4), while the murderer may not. Paul at Athens finds an altar TO THE UNKNOWN GOD and says, “Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” (Act 17:23) — sincerity is granted, and it is not treated as salvation; he goes straight on to say God now commandeth all men every where to repent. And Paul of himself: “who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief” (1Ti 1:13). He does not say his ignorance excused him; he says it was the occasion of mercy, and calls himself in the next breath the chief of sinners.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ignorantly as without knowledge, instruction or information; unwittingly.
webster_full: IGNORANTLY, adv. Without knowledge, instruction or information.
Whom ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. Acts xvii.
IGNORANCE, n. Want of knowledge or information respecting any thing.
scriptures: And the priest shall make an atonement for the soul that sinneth ignorantly, when he sinneth by ignorance before the LORD, to make an atonement for him; and it shall be forgiven him.
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
corruption_summary: Sincerity has been promoted to the status of a saving qualification, so that the man who worships something is thought to be worshipping God under another name — which is exactly the claim Paul declined to make at Athens.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17:23 is the favourite proof text of religious inclusivism, and it will not carry the weight. Paul saw an altar to an unknown God and used it as an opening: whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. Inclusivism reads this as a concession — the Athenians were already worshipping the true God imperfectly, and Paul merely supplied the correct name. But read the rest of the sermon. He tells them God dwelleth not in temples made with hands; that the Godhead is not like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device; that the times of this ignorance God winked at, but now commandeth all men every where to repent; and that He hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained. That is not a validation of Athenian religion. It is a demand that Athens abandon it, addressed to people whose ignorance Paul explicitly names as ignorance. The Numbers 15 pattern is the right frame for the whole subject: the sin of ignorance is real sin, requiring real atonement, and God graciously provides one. Paul's own testimony says the same thing about himself — he did it ignorantly in unbelief, and he obtained mercy, and he was still a blasphemer and a persecutor who needed it. Ignorance in Scripture is never innocence. It is the condition in which mercy finds a man.
roots_summary: Hebrew shegagah (H7684), an error, an unwitting sin; bibliy da'ath, without knowledge, of the manslayer; Greek agnoeo (G50), to be ignorant, not to know.
roots_lines: Hebrew shegagah (H7684) — an inadvertence, a sin of error; the whole class of sins for which the sin offering was appointed; Numbers 15:24-29, Leviticus 4:2.
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant, not to know; Paul's word for his own former state, and the root of agnostos, the unknown God of the altar; 1 Timothy 1:13, Acts 17:23.
Greek agnoia (G52) — ignorance; the times of this ignorance God winked at, but now commandeth all men every where to repent; Acts 17:30, Ephesians 4:18.
usage: “An atonement for the soul that sinneth ignorantly” — a real sin, and a real sacrifice.
“Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” — an opening, not a validation.
“I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief” — the occasion of mercy, not an excuse.

pos: adv. (luxuriously; in ease and softness; also, of a manner, daintily or affectedly)
etymology: Latin delicatus, giving pleasure, luxurious. In the Authorized Version the word almost always names a life of ease, and almost always with a sting.
biblical_def: Agag came to Samuel “delicately”, saying, Surely the bitterness of death is past (1Sa 15:32) — a king walking in daintily, sure he had escaped, and Samuel hewed him in pieces before the LORD. Solomon warns about softness in the training of a household: “He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length” (Pro 29:21) — indulgence blurs an order it was meant to serve. Jeremiah's lament over the siege of Jerusalem is the most terrible: “They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills” (Lam 4:5). And the Lord Jesus uses the word to distinguish John the Baptist from the court: what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? “Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts” (Luk 7:25). John was in a prison, not a palace, and the Lord added that among those that are born of women there is not a greater prophet. Scripture does not condemn comfort as such — it gives wine that maketh glad the heart of man — but it never once presents a delicate life as a strong one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines delicately as in a delicate manner; with nice regard to propriety; daintily; luxuriously; and, of rearing, tenderly, effeminately.
webster_full: DELICATELY, adv. In a delicate manner; with nice regard to propriety and the feelings of others.
2. Daintily; luxuriously.
3. With nice regard to the shape and appearance; tenderly; effeminately.
scriptures: He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length.
Lam 4:5
They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills.
Luk 7:25
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts.
corruption_summary: Comfort has become the unexamined goal of an entire civilisation, and a church shaped by that goal produces converts who have never been asked to bear anything.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 7:24-28 is a deliberate contrast, and the Lord draws it Himself. He asks the crowd what they went into the wilderness to see: a reed shaken with the wind? a man clothed in soft raiment? and answers His own question — they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts. John was not in a king's court. He was in a king's prison, for telling that king he could not have his brother's wife, and he would shortly lose his head for it. And of that man the Lord says there is not a greater prophet born of women. Scripture is not ascetic; it forbids the doctrine that commands to abstain from meats which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving, and it fills the promised land with milk and honey. But it consistently declines to treat comfort as an achievement or a proof of favour. A church that has quietly adopted comfort as its organising assumption — in its preaching, its programmes, its expectations of the Christian life — will produce members who have never been asked to endure anything, and it will not be able to explain to them what has happened when suffering arrives, as Lamentations 4:5 says it does: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills. Paul's charge to Timothy has no equivalent in that vocabulary: thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'adan (H4574), delicacies, dainties; panaq (H6445), to pamper, to bring up delicately; Greek truphe (G5172), luxury, soft living.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'adan (H4574) — dainties, delicacies; those who fed delicately, now desolate in the streets; Lamentations 4:5, 1 Samuel 15:32.
Hebrew panaq (H6445) — to pamper, to indulge; used once, of the servant brought up delicately from a child; Proverbs 29:21.
Greek truphe (G5172) — softness, luxury, delicate living; the courts of kings, and the riotous living Peter condemns; Luke 7:25, 2 Peter 2:13.
usage: “And Agag came unto him delicately” — a king walking in daintily, sure the bitterness of death was past.
“They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets” — the siege of Jerusalem.
“They which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts” — and John was in a prison.

pos: adv. (clearly; without disguise or obscurity; in words that need no interpreter)
etymology: Latin planus, level, flat, clear. To speak plainly is to speak on level ground — nothing raised up to be climbed over, nothing hidden in a hollow.
biblical_def: The bondservant who chooses perpetual service must “plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exo 21:5) — a life-altering commitment must be spoken in unmistakable words before witnesses. The law itself was to be published the same way: “thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly” (Deu 27:8), on plaistered stones at Ebal, where any Israelite could read them. God's dealings with men are described in the same terms: “Did I plainly appear unto the house of thy father, when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh's house?” (1Sa 2:27), the man of God to Eli, arguing from a revelation that had not been obscure. And plainness can be selective: Saul told his uncle plainly that the asses were found, “but of the matter of the kingdom, whereof Samuel spake, he told him not” (1Sa 10:16). In the New Testament the Lord tells the disciples plainly that Lazarus is dead, and speaks of the hour when He shall shew them plainly of the Father; and Paul makes plainness a matter of ministerial conscience: we use great plainness of speech, and are not as many, which corrupt the word of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plainly as without gloss or disguise; clearly; evidently; in a manner to be easily understood; frankly; honestly.
webster_full: PLAINLY, adv. Without glosses or disguise; honestly; sincerely.
2. In a manner to be easily seen or comprehended.
3. Frankly; candidly; without reserve; as, tell me plainly what you think.
scriptures: Deu 27:8
And thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly.
Exo 21:5
And if the servant shall plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free:
Seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech:
corruption_summary: Preaching that leaves the hearer uncertain what was claimed is now often praised as thoughtful, and Scripture treats plainness as a duty of the messenger rather than a defect of style.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 27:8 is a small command with a large principle: write it very plainly. The stones at Ebal were plaistered and inscribed so that the law could be read by farmers and shepherds standing in a field, not decoded by a class of interpreters. That is the Bible's own instinct about its own words, and it is the doctrine the Reformers called the perspicuity of Scripture — not that every passage is equally easy, which the Confession expressly denies, but that the things necessary to be known, believed and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded that not only the learned but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain a sufficient understanding of them. Two opposite corruptions attack it. The older is the priestly one, which keeps the text in a language the people cannot read and reserves its meaning to a hierarchy; the Reformation answered it with translation. The newer is a habit of preaching and writing in which nothing is ever quite asserted — the sermon raises questions, offers perspectives, and closes without the hearer being able to say what the preacher claimed — and this is often mistaken for humility and depth. Paul's standard is plainness of speech, and he grounds it in confidence rather than arrogance: seeing then that we have such hope, we use great plainness of speech. A man who is sure of his message can afford to be understood.
roots_summary: Hebrew ba'ar (H874), to make plain, to engrave distinctly; Greek parrhesia (G3954), freedom of speech, boldness, plainness; Greek saphos, clearly.
roots_lines: Hebrew ba'ar (H874) — to make distinct, to engrave plainly; the law on the stones at Ebal, and the vision written that he may run that readeth it; Deuteronomy 27:8, Habakkuk 2:2.

Greek parrhesia (G3954) — all-speech, freedom to say everything; rendered plainness, boldness, and confidence, of the apostles and of the believer's access; 2 Corinthians 3:12, Acts 4:13, Hebrews 4:16.
Hebrew infinitive absolute construction — the doubling that gives “plainly say” and “plainly appear” their emphatic force; Exodus 21:5, 1 Samuel 2:27.
usage: “Write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly” — readable in a field.
“If the servant shall plainly say” — a life-altering choice spoken in unmistakable words.
“We use great plainness of speech” — plainness grounded in confidence.

pos: adv. (in a peaceable manner; without hostility; of speech, of approach, and of the Christian's dealings with all men)
etymology: Latin pax, peace. The Hebrew idiom is literally “to speak to a man for peace” — the question is not tone but intention.
biblical_def: The first use is a diagnosis of a household: Joseph's brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, “and they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him” (Gen 37:4). The inability is the symptom; the pit and the caravan follow. Then a border dispute: the king of Ammon demands of Jephthah, “now therefore restore those lands again peaceably” (Jdg 11:13) — a demand framed as an offer of peace, and Jephthah answers it with three hundred years of history. Then a mission of reconciliation after a civil war: the congregation “sent some to speak to the children of Benjamin that were in the rock Rimmon, and to call peaceably unto them” (Jdg 21:13). And then the frightened elders of Bethlehem meeting a prophet who has come to anoint a king: “Comest thou peaceably?” (1Sa 16:4). Paul gathers the whole matter into the rule for Christians: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men (Rom 12:18). Both qualifications are in that verse and both are deliberate — if it be possible, because it will not always be; and as much as lieth in you, because the failure must never be on our side.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines peaceably as without war, tumult or private feuds; without disturbance; quietly; without agitation.
webster_full: PEACEABLY, adv. Without war; without tumult or commotion; without private feuds and quarrels.
2. Without disturbance; quietly; without agitation; without interruption.
PEACEABLE, a. Free from war, tumult or public commotion; quiet; undisturbed.
scriptures: Gen 37:4
And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.
And Samuel did that which the LORD spake, and came to Bethlehem. And the elders of the town trembled at his coming, and said, Comest thou peaceably?
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
corruption_summary: Romans 12:18 is quoted without its two qualifiers, producing a peace that is really conflict-avoidance, and a church that will surrender any truth rather than have an argument.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul wrote a sentence with two safety catches on it, and both are regularly filed off in quotation. If it be possible concedes that it will not always be possible — and the same apostle withstood Peter to the face, delivered a man to Satan, named Hymenaeus and Alexander and Demas, and pronounced anathema on preachers of another gospel. As much as lieth in you puts the whole burden on our side of the line, so that a Christian may be at odds with a man only when the other party has made peace impossible, never because he could not be bothered to try. What is commonly practised instead is a third thing that Scripture nowhere commends: conflict-avoidance, in which peace is preserved by declining to say anything that would provoke, and the price is paid in truths not stated, sins not addressed, and errors left standing in the congregation. James 3:17 gives the ordering that governs the whole subject — the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable. Purity first. A peace bought by abandoning purity is not the peace James means, and Jeremiah's prophets who cried Peace, peace, when there was no peace were not peacemakers but liars. Genesis 37:4 shows the opposite failure and it is just as real: a family in which the brothers could not speak peaceably, and a father whose favouritism had made the household ungovernable.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness, welfare; the idiom dabar l'shalom, to speak for peace; Greek eireneuo (G1514), to be at peace, to live peaceably.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, completeness, welfare; the brothers who could not speak for peace, and the elders' question at Bethlehem; Genesis 37:4, 1 Samuel 16:4.
Greek eireneuo (G1514) — to be at peace, to live in peace; Paul's qualified command, and be at peace among yourselves; Romans 12:18, 1 Thessalonians 5:13.
Greek eirenikos (G1516) — peaceable; the wisdom from above, which is first pure, then peaceable; James 3:17.
usage: “They hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him” — the symptom before the pit.
“Comest thou peaceably?” — elders trembling at a prophet's arrival.
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you” — two qualifiers, both deliberate.

pos: adv. (with pride; arrogantly; in Scripture, chiefly in the phrase “dealt proudly”, of men setting themselves against God)
etymology: Old French prud, valiant, which in English took on the sense of overweening. The Hebrew zud means to boil up, to seethe over — pride as a pot that has risen past its rim.
biblical_def: The phrase “dealt proudly” is the Bible's standing formula for a settled contempt of God, and Jethro coins it: “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods: for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them” (Exo 18:11) — Egypt drowned in the very water she had used to drown the Hebrew children. Hannah warns against it in her song: “Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed” (1Sa 2:3). The Levites in Nehemiah's great prayer of confession use it twice, and the second use is the point: God shewed signs and wonders upon Pharaoh, “for thou knewest that they dealt proudly against them” (Neh 9:10) — and then, of Israel herself, “But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments” (Neh 9:16). The identical charge is laid against Egypt and against the covenant people, in one chapter, in the same words. That is the argument of the whole prayer: God is just in all that is brought upon us, for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines proudly as with an air of superiority; haughtily; ostentatiously; arrogantly; in defiance of authority.
webster_full: PROUDLY, adv. With an air of superiority; haughtily; ostentatiously.
2. Arrogantly; in defiance of law or authority.
Talk no more so exceeding proudly. 1 Sam. ii.
scriptures: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods: for in the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them.
Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
Neh 9:16
But they and our fathers dealt proudly, and hardened their necks, and hearkened not to thy commandments,
corruption_summary: Pride has been reclassified as a virtue and adopted as a public banner, while the Christian counterfeit — a doctrinal party that despises everyone outside it — goes largely unnamed.
corruption_paragraphs: Pride is the one sin our culture has promoted to a public celebration, and it is worth being precise about what the Bible means by the word, because equivocation runs in both directions. Scripture does not condemn the honest satisfaction of a man in good work — let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone. What it condemns, in the phrase dealt proudly, is the seething-over of a creature against his Maker: the refusal of the place a man has been given, the hardened neck, the arrogancy out of the mouth. God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace unto the humble, and Proverbs sets a proud look at the head of the list of six things the LORD doth hate. That much is easy for a confessional church to say. The harder word is the one Nehemiah 9 forces, where the same charge falls on Egypt and on Israel in the same chapter, in the same words. A Reformed congregation is not automatically on the humble side of that ledger. The doctrines of grace, of all doctrines, ought to make a man least able to look down on anyone — who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? — and where they have instead produced a party that despises the ignorant, the charismatic, the Arminian, and the unlearned, that is not orthodoxy. It is dealing proudly, and Hannah's warning is addressed to it: by him actions are weighed.
roots_summary: Hebrew zud (H2102), to boil up, to seethe, to act presumptuously; ga'on (H1347), majesty, and so arrogance; Greek huperephanos (G5244), showing oneself above others.
roots_lines: Hebrew zud (H2102) — to boil up, to act presumptuously or proudly; the standing verb of the phrase “dealt proudly”, of Egypt and of Israel; Exodus 18:11, Nehemiah 9:10, 9:16.
Hebrew ga'on (H1347) — exaltation, majesty, and so arrogance; pride goeth before destruction; Proverbs 16:18, Isaiah 2:12.
Greek huperephanos (G5244) — appearing above others, haughty; God resisteth the proud, quoted twice from Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5.
usage: “In the thing wherein they dealt proudly he was above them” — Egypt drowned in her own instrument.
“Talk no more so exceeding proudly…by him actions are weighed” — Hannah's song.
“They and our fathers dealt proudly” — the same charge, the same chapter, the covenant people.

pos: adv. (with force; by seizure; in the law, of goods taken away by strength rather than by right)
etymology: Latin violentus, forcible, from vis, force. The Authorized Version's recurring phrase is “violently taken away”, rendering the Hebrew gazal, to tear off, to seize.
biblical_def: The word is chiefly a legal term for property seized. Abraham “reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away” (Gen 21:25) — and the two men made a covenant at Beersheba over it, so that the dispute ended in an oath rather than a feud. The law of the trespass offering names the sin and prescribes restitution with a fifth part added: “he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found” (Lev 6:4). Notice the range: robbery, fraud, breach of trust, and keeping what you found, all in one verse, all requiring restitution and a ram for a trespass offering — God is not satisfied by the sacrifice alone, and the neighbour must be paid. The covenant curses use the phrase for the reversal of ownership under judgment: “thine ass shall be violently taken away from before thy face, and shall not be restored to thee” (Deu 28:31). And Zophar states the principle over the oppressor: “because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor; because he hath violently taken away an house which he builded not” (Job 20:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines violently as with force; forcibly; with great force or vehemence; and, of taking, by unjust force or seizure.
webster_full: VIOLENTLY, adv. With force; forcibly; vehemently.
2. With unjust force; by seizure.
He shall restore that which he took violently away. Lev. vi.
scriptures: And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away.
Lev 6:4

Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that which was delivered him to keep, or the lost thing which he found,
Luk 19:8
And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
corruption_summary: Repentance is widely preached as a change of heart with no obligation to the person wronged, and the trespass offering required both the sacrifice and the money back with a fifth added.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 6 is the passage that will not let repentance stay private. A man who has robbed, defrauded, broken a trust, or kept what he found must do three things: restore the principal, add a fifth part more, and bring a ram to the priest for a trespass offering. The sacrifice does not replace the restitution and the restitution does not replace the sacrifice. That order survives into the New Testament intact. Zacchaeus, in the hour of his conversion, does the arithmetic aloud — half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he has defrauded — and the Lord's response is, This day is salvation come to this house. Nothing in that transaction purchases his salvation; the restitution is the evidence of it, and the Lord names it as such. Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon and offers to pay whatever the runaway owes: put that on mine account; I will repay it. What is commonly preached instead is a repentance consisting entirely of inward sorrow and a settled peace with God, with the injured party never contacted and the money never returned, on the reasoning that the debt has been dealt with at the cross. The cross deals with the guilt. It does not cancel the neighbour's well, or his wages, or his house. The 1689 Confession says of repentance that the penitent is to endeavour to walk before God unto all well-pleasing in all things — and restitution is where that endeavour becomes visible and expensive.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazal (H1497), to tear away, to seize, to rob by force; 'ashaq (H6231), to oppress, to defraud; shuwb (H7725), to return or restore — the verb of restitution.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear off, to seize, to take by violence; the well at Beersheba and the house the oppressor did not build; Genesis 21:25, Job 20:19.
Hebrew 'ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, to defraud, to withhold wages; joined with gazal throughout the law and prophets; Leviticus 6:2, Micah 2:2.
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to restore; the same verb serves for returning stolen goods and for turning to the LORD; Leviticus 6:4, Hosea 14:1.
usage: “A well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away” — a dispute that ended in an oath.
“He shall restore that which he took violently away” — and add a fifth part.
“I restore him fourfold” — repentance doing arithmetic out loud.

pos: adv. (with great force or eagerness; violently; of a stream, a protest, and an interrogation)
etymology: Latin vehemens, eager, impetuous. In the Authorized Version it is used of natural force and of human intensity, and the two are set against each other in one parable.
biblical_def: Peter, told that he would deny his Lord thrice, “spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all” (Mar 14:31). The vehemence was sincere and it was worthless; within hours he was cursing and swearing at a fire. In the parable of the two builders the word describes the flood: the wise man “digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it” (Luk 6:48); and of the other, “against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great” (Luk 6:49). Both houses met the same stream. The difference was invisible until the day it was tested, because a foundation is by definition the part nobody sees. And the scribes and Pharisees, after the woes, “began to urge him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak of many things” (Luk 11:53), laying wait for him and seeking to catch something out of his mouth. Three vehemences: a disciple's failed resolve, a river's real force, and an enemy's interrogation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vehemently as with great force or violence; forcibly; with animation or fervor; urgently.
webster_full: VEHEMENTLY, adv. With great force or violence; forcibly.
2. With great animation, ardor or fervor; urgently.
VEHEMENT, a. Very forcible; violent; acting with great force; ardent; eager.
scriptures: But he spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all.
Luk 6:48

He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.
Luk 6:49

But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.
corruption_summary: Sincere intensity is repeatedly mistaken for spiritual strength, and Peter at the table is the standing proof that a man may mean every word of a vow he cannot keep.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 14:31 is a merciful verse to have in the Bible. Peter did not lie. He spoke the more vehemently, and he meant it: If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all — the whole company, unanimous and fervent. Hours later one of them was cursing by a fire and the rest had fled. The lesson is not that Peter was a hypocrite; it is that the strength of a resolution is no measure of the strength of the man who makes it. Modern Christian practice is full of vehemence taken as evidence: the intensity of a response at a meeting, the fervour of a public commitment, the conviction with which something is said. Luke 6:48-49 puts the true test in a different place entirely. Two houses, one storm, the same stream beating vehemently on both, and the difference is a foundation dug deep and laid on rock — work done long before, out of sight, and not visible on the day it was done. And the Lord names the foundation plainly in the same paragraph: whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them. It is not hearing that founds a house, and it is not feeling. Peter's restoration is the other half of the mercy: the man who failed his own vow at the fire was given a threefold charge by another fire and fed the sheep for thirty years.
roots_summary: Greek ekperissos (G4057 intensive), exceedingly, more vehemently; prosregnumi (G4366), to break upon, of the stream against the house; deinos (G1171), terribly, vehemently.
roots_lines: Greek ekperissos — exceedingly, beyond measure; Peter speaking the more vehemently; Mark 14:31.
Greek prosregnumi (G4366) — to break or burst upon; the flood breaking on both houses; Luke 6:48-49.
Greek deinos (G1171) — terribly, grievously, vehemently; the scribes and Pharisees urging Him and laying wait; Luke 11:53.
usage: “He spake the more vehemently” — sincere, unanimous, and worthless by morning.
“The stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it” — the same storm on both houses.
“Began to urge him vehemently” — interrogation as a trap.

pos: adv. (heavily; sorely; with great weight of affliction or of guilt)
etymology: Latin gravis, heavy, through Old French grever, to burden. The word is about weight before it is about sorrow: a grievous thing is a heavy thing.
biblical_def: Isaiah uses it of God's dealings with the north: the dimness shall not be such as it was, “when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations” (Isa 9:1) — and the very next verse is the promise Matthew quotes of Christ's Galilean ministry: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. The most grievously afflicted region got the Light first. Jeremiah uses it of judgment: a whirlwind of the LORD is gone forth in fury, “it shall fall grievously upon the head of the wicked” (Jer 23:19). And Lamentations uses it twice of sin, in a first-person confession: “Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed” (Lam 1:8), and “mine heart is turned within me; for I have grievously rebelled” (Lam 1:20). That is the right order in Scripture: the affliction is named as heavy, the sin that brought it is named as heavy, and the same book that says I have grievously rebelled says his compassions fail not, they are new every morning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grievously as with pain or distress; with great uneasiness; calamitously; in a manner to give great weight or offense.
webster_full: GRIEVOUSLY, adv. With pain or distress; as, to be grievously afflicted.
2. With discontent or ill will.
3. Calamitously; miserably; with great uneasiness or grief.
scriptures: Isa 9:1

Nevertheless the dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.
Lam 1:20
Behold, O LORD; for I am in distress: my bowels are troubled; mine heart is turned within me; for I have grievously rebelled: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home there is as death.
Isa 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
corruption_summary: Sin is graded by its social consequences rather than by the God against whom it is committed, and Scripture's language of grievous sin is accordingly heard as exaggeration.
corruption_paragraphs: Lamentations 1:8 and 1:20 use the strongest available word about the speaker's own nation and the speaker's own heart: Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; I have grievously rebelled. That vocabulary is now nearly unusable, because sin is popularly weighed by the harm it does to other people, and by that measure most sin is light. Scripture weighs it by the One against whom it is done. David, who had committed adultery and arranged a murder, prayed, Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight — not because Uriah and Bathsheba were nothing, but because the weight of the offence is set by the majesty of the offended. Joseph asks the same question in Potiphar's house: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? The practical effect of the modern scale is a Christianity in which small sins are unconfessable because there is nothing to confess and large sins are unbearable because there is no proportionate remedy. The biblical scale gives a heavier weight and a heavier remedy in the same book. Lamentations 3 is the same author, forty verses later: it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. And Isaiah 9 is the pattern in miniature — the region most grievously afflicted is the region where the great light shone first.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabad (H3513), to be heavy, weighty, grievous; marad (H4775), to rebel; chata' (H2398), to sin, to miss the mark.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy or weighty; the same root gives kabod, glory, so that weight is the common idea in both affliction and honour; Isaiah 9:1, Exodus 5:9.
Hebrew marad (H4775) — to rebel, to revolt; the confession of Lamentations 1:20 and the charge against Israel in the wilderness; Numbers 14:9.
Hebrew chata' (H2398) — to miss the mark, to sin; Jerusalem hath grievously sinned, an emphatic doubling of the verb; Lamentations 1:8.
usage: “Afterward did more grievously afflict her…in Galilee of the nations” — and the light shone there first.
“Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed” — the cause named plainly.
“For I have grievously rebelled” — first person, in the same book as new every morning.

pos: adv. (harshly; with severity of manner or speech)
etymology: Old English ruh, rough, rugged. In the Authorized Version rough speech appears three times, and the three occasions could hardly be more different in motive.
biblical_def: Joseph, seeing his brethren after twenty years, “made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them” (Gen 42:7), and they reported it at home: “The man, who is the lord of the land, spake roughly to us, and took us for spies” (Gen 42:30). The roughness was assumed, sustained through two journeys, a silver cup and a threatened enslavement, and it ended with Joseph weeping so loudly that the house of Pharaoh heard it. It was a surgeon's roughness: it brought the brothers to say among themselves, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, and it tested whether they would abandon Benjamin as they had abandoned him. David fears a different roughness: “what if thy father answer thee roughly?” (1Sa 20:10) — and Saul answered Jonathan by throwing a javelin at him. And Rehoboam supplies the third: “the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men's counsel that they gave him” (1Ki 12:13), telling Israel his little finger should be thicker than his father's loins — and ten tribes walked out of the kingdom. Roughness in the service of reconciliation restored a family; roughness in the service of pride destroyed a nation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines roughly as with uneven surface; harshly; uncivilly; rudely; severely; without tenderness or delicacy.
webster_full: ROUGHLY, adv. With uneven surface; with asperity of surface.
2. Harshly; uncivilly; rudely; as, to be treated roughly.
3. Severely; without tenderness; as, to blame too roughly.
scriptures: Gen 42:7

And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them; and he said unto them, Whence come ye? And they said, From the land of Canaan to buy food.
And the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men's counsel that they gave him;
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
corruption_summary: Harshness is defended as honesty and gentleness dismissed as compromise, when Scripture judges the manner of a word by whether it was aimed at the hearer's good or the speaker's standing.
corruption_paragraphs: Set Joseph beside Rehoboam and the whole question of hard speech is settled. Both men spoke roughly. Joseph did it deliberately, to men who deserved far worse, and every hard word was aimed at bringing them to the confession he finally heard through an interpreter: We are verily guilty concerning our brother. He was in the room when they said it, and he turned himself about from them and wept. Rehoboam did it to men who had asked him a fair question, on the advice of his contemporaries, against the counsel of the old men who had stood before Solomon, and his object was to establish that he was not to be trifled with. The first roughness produced a reconciled family and a nation preserved through famine; the second split the kingdom in a day. Scripture therefore refuses both of the easy modern positions. It will not say that hard words are always wrong — the prophets are full of them, and the Lord called Herod a fox and the Pharisees whited sepulchres. And it will not let a man plead prophetic bluntness as a cover for temper: a soft answer turneth away wrath, and the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men. The question Scripture asks about a hard word is not whether it was true but what it was for — the hearer's repentance, or the speaker's standing.
roots_summary: Hebrew qasheh (H7186), hard, severe, harsh; 'anah qashot, to answer roughly; rak (H7390), soft, tender — the soft answer of Proverbs 15:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew qasheh (H7186) — hard, severe, stiff; used of Joseph's assumed harshness, Rehoboam's answer, and a stiffnecked people; Genesis 42:7, 1 Kings 12:13, Exodus 32:9.
Hebrew rak (H7390) — soft, tender, gentle; the soft answer that turns away wrath; Proverbs 15:1, Genesis 33:13.
Greek epieikes (G1933) — gentle, forbearing, moderate; required of a bishop and of the servant of the Lord; 1 Timothy 3:3, Titus 3:2.
usage: “Made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly” — a surgeon's harshness, and a house that heard him weep.
“What if thy father answer thee roughly?” — and Saul threw a javelin.
“The king answered the people roughly” — and ten tribes walked out.

pos: adv. (gently; quietly; at a slow pace; also, of movement, stealthily)
etymology: Old English softe, gentle, agreeable. The Authorized Version uses the word for gentleness of pace, of tread, and of a humbled walk.
biblical_def: Jacob, asked by Esau to travel together, declines on behalf of the weak: “I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure” (Gen 33:14). The pace of the company is set by its slowest member, and Isaiah says the same of the LORD, who shall gently lead those that are with young. Then two scenes of stealth. Jael “took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him” (Jdg 4:21). And Ruth, on Naomi's instruction, “came softly, and uncovered his feet, and laid her down” at the threshingfloor (Rut 3:7) — a widow asking a kinsman, in the customary manner of that place, to spread his skirt over her and act as redeemer, and Boaz's first words are a blessing on her for it. Finally, the most surprising use of all: “when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly” (1Ki 21:27). Ahab, of whom it is written that there was none like him who sold himself to work wickedness, walked softly — and God said to Elijah, Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? and deferred the evil to his son's days.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines softly as without noise or violence; gently; quietly; with a slow pace or motion; mildly; tenderly.
webster_full: SOFTLY, adv. Without noise or violence; gently.
He came softly to the door.
2. Not loudly; without noise. 3. Gently; placidly. 4. Mildly; tenderly.
scriptures: Let my lord, I pray thee, pass over before his servant: and I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure, until I come unto my lord unto Seir.
And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.
Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me? because he humbleth himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days: but in his son's days will I bring the evil upon his house.
corruption_summary: Church life is organised around the pace of its strongest members, and Genesis 33:14 sets the opposite rule — the company moves at the speed of the children and the nursing flocks.
corruption_paragraphs: Jacob's sentence is one of the finest pastoral texts in the Old Testament and it is almost never preached as one: I will lead on softly, according as the cattle that goeth before me and the children be able to endure. He had every reason to hurry — an armed brother, four hundred men, a long-feared reckoning just survived — and he set his pace by nursing ewes and small children. Isaiah gives the same picture of God Himself: he shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young. Paul builds his whole argument about liberty in Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 on the same principle, and states it flatly: we then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. The ordinary shape of church life runs the other way. Programmes, teaching, expectations, and pace are set by the healthy, the able, the free of encumbrance, and those who cannot keep up quietly stop coming: the family with a disabled child, the widow who cannot drive at night, the new convert who does not know the vocabulary, the man working two shifts. Ahab, meanwhile, walking softly in sackcloth, is the standing reminder that God notices even a hypocrite's humbling — which ought to make the church slow to write anybody off.
roots_summary: Hebrew la'at (H328), softly, gently, secretly; 'at (H328 variant), slowly; nahal (H5095), to lead gently, as with young.
roots_lines: Hebrew la'at / 'at (H328) — softly, gently, secretly; Jacob's pace, Jael's tread, Ruth at the threshingfloor, and Ahab in sackcloth; Genesis 33:14, Judges 4:21, Ruth 3:7, 1 Kings 21:27.
Hebrew nahal (H5095) — to lead gently, to guide to a watering place; he leadeth me beside the still waters, and gently leads those with young; Psalm 23:2, Isaiah 40:11.
Hebrew kana' (H3665) — to humble oneself, to be brought low; the verb of Ahab's reprieve and of 2 Chronicles 7:14; 1 Kings 21:29, 2 Chronicles 7:14.
usage: “I will lead on softly…as the children be able to endure” — the pace set by the weakest.
“She came softly, and uncovered his feet” — a widow claiming a redeemer.
“And went softly” — and God said, Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself?

pos: adv. (with pleasure; willingly; of hearing and receiving the word)
etymology: Old English glæd, bright, cheerful. The Authorized Version attaches the word repeatedly to hearing, and the results are instructive.
biblical_def: Herod is the warning: “Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly” (Mar 6:20). He feared the preacher, protected him, obeyed him in many things, and enjoyed listening — and beheaded him at a birthday party for a girl's dance. Gladness in hearing is not conversion. Of the Lord's own preaching: “the common people heard him gladly” (Mar 12:37), and Luke says that on His return from Gadara “the people gladly received him: for they were all waiting for him” (Luk 8:40). But the decisive use is Pentecost: “they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls” (Act 2:41) — and there the gladness was preceded by pricked hearts and the question Men and brethren, what shall we do?, and was followed by repentance, baptism, and continuing steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship. The difference between Herod and Pentecost is not the quality of the hearing; both were glad. It is what came after the sermon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gladly as with pleasure; joyfully; cheerfully; willingly.
webster_full: GLADLY, adv. With pleasure; joyfully; cheerfully.
The common people heard him gladly. Mark xii.
GLAD, a. Pleased; affected with pleasure or moderate joy; cheerful.
scriptures: Mar 6:20
For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy, and observed him; and when he heard him, he did many things, and heard him gladly.
David therefore himself calleth him Lord; and whence is he then his son? And the common people heard him gladly.
Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
corruption_summary: Enjoyment of preaching is widely accepted as evidence of spiritual health, and Mark 6:20 records a man who enjoyed the best preacher of his generation and murdered him.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 6:20 ought to be read at the door of every popular ministry. Herod heard John gladly. He also feared him, knew him to be a just man and an holy, kept him safe from Herodias, and did many things at his word. On any modern measure of engagement, Herod was a model listener: attentive, respectful, responsive, and personally fond of the preacher. Then a girl danced, an oath was made in front of guests, and John's head came in on a charger. The Lord's parable of the sower names the type — he that received the seed into stony places is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while. Gladness is explicitly listed there as a feature of the soil that fails. This matters because the church has largely adopted enjoyment as its metric: whether people liked the sermon, whether they were moved, whether they would recommend it. Ezekiel was told what that could mean: thou art unto them as a very lovely song of one that hath a pleasant voice, and can play well on an instrument: for they hear thy words, but they do them not. Acts 2:41 shows the other case and the difference is entirely in the sequel — gladness that ended in baptism, repentance, doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers. The test of a hearing is never the hour it happened in. It is the month afterward.
roots_summary: Greek hedeos (G2234), gladly, with pleasure; apodechomai (G588), to receive gladly, to welcome; chara (G5479), joy — including the joy of the stony ground.
roots_lines: Greek hedeos (G2234) — sweetly, gladly, with pleasure; Herod hearing John and the common people hearing Christ; Mark 6:20, 12:37.
Greek apodechomai (G588) — to receive heartily, to welcome; the crowd receiving Jesus, and the three thousand receiving the word; Luke 8:40, Acts 2:41.
Greek chara (G5479) — joy; anon with joy receiveth it, of the stony ground that has no root; Matthew 13:20-21.
usage: “And heard him gladly” — Herod, who also beheaded him.
“The common people heard him gladly” — and many of the same crowd cried Crucify him.
“They that gladly received his word were baptized” — gladness with a sequel.

pos: adv. (in haste; quickly; also, rashly, without due deliberation)
etymology: Old French haste, speed. The Authorized Version uses the word both for a summons that cannot wait and for the rashness Solomon warns against.
biblical_def: Sometimes haste is God's timing: “Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh” (Gen 41:14). After thirteen years, the change took an hour. Sometimes the absence of haste is God's method: “the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua” (Jdg 2:23), and Exodus explains why — lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee: by little and little I will drive them out. Sometimes haste is panic: Abimelech, with a millstone in his skull, “called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer” to run him through, so that men would not say a woman slew him (Jdg 9:54), a man managing his reputation with his last breath. And sometimes haste is the news itself: “the man came in hastily, and told Eli” (1Sa 4:14) that Israel was fled, his sons were dead, and the ark of God was taken. Over all of it stands Solomon's rule for the tongue and the temper: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth, and, be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hastily as in haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly; and also rashly, precipitately, without due reflection.
webster_full: HASTILY, adv. In haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly.
2. Rashly; precipitately; without due reflection.
3. Passionately; under sudden excitement of passion.
scriptures: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.
Jdg 2:23
Therefore the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua.
Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
corruption_summary: Speed is treated as a virtue in itself, and Scripture consistently distinguishes the haste that obeys a summons from the haste that outruns knowledge.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 2:23 says something a results-driven age finds nearly incomprehensible: the LORD left those nations, without driving them out hastily. He could have emptied Canaan in a week; He said He would do it by little and little, and gave two reasons — that the land not become desolate and the wild beasts multiply, and that Israel might be proved and taught war. Sanctification runs on the same principle, and it is the reason God does not remove every sin from a believer at conversion: the ground could not carry it, and the man would learn nothing. Meanwhile Proverbs draws the line on the other side: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth; the thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness, but of every one that is hasty only to want; be not rash with thy mouth; he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. The haste Scripture blesses is obedience to a summons — the shepherds came with haste to Bethlehem, Zacchaeus made haste and came down, David ran toward the giant. The haste it condemns is the haste that outruns knowledge: the vow, the answer, the purchase, the appointment of a novice to office, the marriage entered on a fortnight's acquaintance. The test is not the speed but whether the man knows what he is doing. Joseph came out of the dungeon hastily because God's hour had struck after thirteen years of not striking.
roots_summary: Hebrew ruwts (H7323), to run; mahar (H4116), to hasten, to be rash; 'uwts (H213), to press, to be hasty — the verb of Proverbs 19:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew ruwts (H7323) — to run; they brought Joseph hastily out of the dungeon; Genesis 41:14.
Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, and so to be rash or impetuous; be not rash with thy mouth; Ecclesiastes 5:2, Proverbs 25:8.
Hebrew 'uwts (H213) — to press, urge, be hasty; he that hasteth with his feet sinneth; Proverbs 19:2, 21:5.
usage: “They brought him hastily out of the dungeon” — thirteen years, then one hour.
“Without driving them out hastily” — by little and little, and for a reason.
“He that hasteth with his feet sinneth” — the haste that outruns knowledge.

pos: adv. (with care; diligently; also, in older English, anxiously or with full of care)
etymology: Old English caru, sorrow, anxiety — the older sense survives in the Authorized Version, where to be careful can mean to be anxious. To do a thing carefully is to do it with the whole weight of one's concern on it.
biblical_def: The word governs the covenant condition: “Only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all these commandments which I command thee this day” (Deu 15:5) — the Hebrew is an emphatic doubling, hearkening thou shalt hearken, and the blessing of the release-year law hangs on it. Micah shows care disappointed: “the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem” (Mic 1:12). Paul uses it of a pastoral errand, sending Epaphroditus the more carefully so the Philippians might rejoice (Php 2:28). And Hebrews gives the most solemn use: Esau, “when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears” (Heb 12:17). Esau's tears were real. What he sought carefully and did not find was not forgiveness in the abstract but the reversal of an irrevocable transaction — the birthright he had sold for a meal, and the blessing that went with it. Care is not always enough, and Scripture says so without softening it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines carefully as with care, caution or solicitude; heedfully; watchfully; attentively; and, in the older sense, in a manner that shows concern or anxiety.
webster_full: CAREFULLY, adv. With care, caution or solicitude.
2. Heedfully; watchfully; attentively; as, consider these precepts carefully.
3. In a manner that shows care.
4. Providently; cautiously.
scriptures: Deu 15:5
Only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all these commandments which I command thee this day.
For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
corruption_summary: The English word has split in two since 1611, and readers now hear “be careful for nothing” as a command to be casual when Paul is forbidding anxiety.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has happened is a shift in the language, and it produces a real misreading. In 1611 careful carried its root sense of being full of care in the older meaning of care — anxiety, worry, the burden of concern. So Philippians 4:6, be careful for nothing, means be anxious about nothing, and Martha is told she is careful and troubled about many things, and Paul says he would have the unmarried without carefulness. Modern English has kept only the sense of diligence, so the reader hears a command to be casual, which is the opposite of Paul's intent and cannot survive contact with the same apostle's daily care of all the churches. Both senses are in the Authorized Version and both are godly in their place: careful in the sense of diligent is commanded — carefully hearken, study to shew thyself approved, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace; careful in the sense of anxious is forbidden and given a remedy in the same verse, prayer and supplication with thanksgiving. Hebrews 12:17 is the sober counterweight to both. Esau sought carefully, in every sense of the word, and with tears, and found no place of repentance — because what a man sells cheaply he may not be able to buy back at any price.
roots_summary: Hebrew emphatic infinitive shamoa' tishma', hearkening thou shalt hearken; Greek spoudaioteros (G4708), the more diligently; Greek merimnao (G3309), to be anxious — the older English “careful”.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamoa' tishma' — the doubled infinitive of shama', to hear; rendered “carefully hearken”, the covenant condition; Deuteronomy 15:5, 28:1.
Greek ekzeteo (G1567) — to seek out earnestly; Esau seeking the blessing carefully with tears; Hebrews 12:17.
Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, to be distracted with care; the sense of “be careful for nothing” and of Martha's trouble; Philippians 4:6, Luke 10:41.
usage: “Only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God” — hearkening thou shalt hearken.
“Though he sought it carefully with tears” — Esau, and a transaction that would not reverse.
“Be careful for nothing” — the older English for be anxious about nothing.

pos: adv. (correctly; justly; in a straight manner; famously, of dividing the word of truth)
etymology: Old English rihte, straight. The Greek orthotomeo in 2 Timothy 2:15 is literally to cut straight — a road-maker's or a ploughman's word, not a butcher's.
biblical_def: Esau, robbed of the blessing, makes a bitter pun: “Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times” (Gen 27:36) — the name means heel-catcher, and Esau says the name fits. In the house of Simon the Pharisee the Lord tells the parable of the two debtors and asks which will love most; Simon answers, I suppose that he to whom he forgave most; and Jesus says, “Thou hast rightly judged” (Luk 7:43) — the Pharisee got the doctrine right and had missed the woman at his feet entirely.
