The spies sent to entangle Christ open with flattery that happens to be true: “we know that thou sayest and teachest rightly, neither acceptest thou the person of any, but teachest the way of God truly” (Luk 20:21). And the great charge: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15). The Greek is orthotomeo, to cut a straight line — the image is of a road driven straight through country, or a furrow ploughed true, and the workman is judged by whether the line runs where the ground requires.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rightly as properly; fitly; suitably; according to justice; according to truth or fact; not erroneously; honestly; uprightly.
webster_full: RIGHTLY, adv. Properly; fitly; suitably; as, to be rightly named.
2. According to truth or fact; not erroneously.
3. Honestly; uprightly; as, to judge rightly. 4. Exactly.
scriptures: And he said, Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing. And he said, Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?
Luk 7:43
Simon answered and said, I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most. And he said unto him, Thou hast rightly judged.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: Rightly dividing the word is claimed as a warrant for a dispensational carving of Scripture into disconnected administrations, when the Greek means to cut a straight line, not to cut a text into pieces.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Timothy 2:15 is one of the most frequently misused verses in Paul. The English phrase rightly dividing has been taken to mean the correct partition of Scripture — and in the dispensational scheme, the division of redemptive history into distinct administrations under which God deals with men on different terms, with a body of teaching assigned to each and much of the Bible thereby set aside as addressed to somebody else. The Greek word will not carry it. Orthotomeo occurs once in the New Testament and means to cut straight: to drive a road straight, to plough a straight furrow, to make a true line. Its opposite in the passage is not bad partitioning but crooked handling, and the very next verses name what Paul had in mind — shun profane and vain babblings, and Hymenaeus and Philetus, who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already. A workman rightly dividing is one whose teaching runs straight through the text without a bend put in it for his own convenience. The dictionary rejects dispensational premillennialism as a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, and holds the covenantal unity of Scripture: one people of God, one gospel of grace from Genesis 3:15 forward, one covenant of grace administered in successive ways and consummated in Christ. That is what a straight line through the Bible looks like.
roots_summary: Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight, to make a straight path; orthos (G3717), straight, upright; Hebrew 'aqab (H6117), to take by the heel, to supplant — the name Jacob.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, as a road or a furrow; used once, of the workman handling the word of truth; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek orthos (G3717) — straight, erect; the root also of orthopodeo, to walk uprightly according to the truth of the gospel; Galatians 2:14, Hebrews 12:13.
Hebrew 'aqab (H6117) — to take by the heel, to supplant, to circumvent; the root of the name Jacob and of Esau's bitter pun; Genesis 27:36, Hosea 12:3.
usage: “Is not he rightly named Jacob?” — a bitter pun on a heel-catcher.
“Thou hast rightly judged” — a Pharisee correct in doctrine and blind to the woman at his feet.
“Rightly dividing the word of truth” — cutting a straight line, not cutting the Bible into pieces.

pos: adv. (with little weight; slightly; and chiefly, in the phrase “lightly esteemed”, to hold in low regard)
etymology: Old English leohte, of little weight. The Authorized Version's use turns almost entirely on weight: to esteem lightly is to assign a thing too little mass.
biblical_def: Abimelech rebukes Abraham for the half-truth about Sarah: “one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us” (Gen 26:10) — a pagan king explaining sin and guilt to a patriarch. The song of Moses gives the classic phrase: “Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked…then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deu 32:15). Prosperity does not usually produce open atheism; it produces a lowered estimate. Then the sentence on the house of Eli, and it is the pivot of the whole story: “them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed” (1Sa 2:30). Eli had honoured his sons above God, and the reciprocity is exact. And David, offered a king's daughter, answers out of a true estimate of himself: “Seemeth it to you a light thing to be a king's son in law, seeing that I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed?” (1Sa 18:23). The man God had already anointed thought himself of no account — and it is worth setting his self-estimate beside Jeshurun's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lightly as with little weight; without deep impression; easily; readily; without reason; and, of esteem, with slight regard.
webster_full: LIGHTLY, adv. With little weight; as, to tread lightly.
2. Without deep impression.
3. Easily; readily; without difficulty. 4. Without reason, or for reasons of little weight. 5. Not chastely.
scriptures: But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.

Wherefore the LORD God of Israel saith, I said indeed that thy house, and the house of thy father, should walk before me for ever: but now the LORD saith, Be it far from me; for them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
And Saul's servants spake those words in the ears of David. And David said, Seemeth it to you a light thing to be a king's son in law, seeing that I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed?
corruption_summary: Apostasy in a prosperous society almost never arrives as denial; it arrives as a lowered estimate, and Deuteronomy 32:15 describes the mechanism exactly.
corruption_paragraphs: The song of Moses predicted the collapse of a nation four decades before the nation entered the land, and it did not predict that Israel would be argued out of her faith. Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked; thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation. Three verbs of prosperity, then two of abandonment, and the second of those is the key: not denied, not disproved — lightly esteemed. The estimate fell. God became a smaller consideration among larger ones, and the practical forsaking followed the change in weight. That is the actual shape of secularisation in the comfortable West, and it explains why apologetic arguments so often miss: most people who have drifted from the faith did not lose an argument. They came to weigh God less, gradually, in a life where He was needed less often, and the doctrinal detachment came afterwards as a tidying-up. Deuteronomy 8 gives the same warning in advance, and the remedy with it: when thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God. The counterweight is deliberate, repeated, spoken thanksgiving in the seasons when nothing is lacking — which is precisely when it feels least necessary. And 1 Samuel 2:30 states the reciprocity plainly: them that honour me I will honour.
roots_summary: Hebrew qalal (H7043), to be slight, to make light of, to curse; nabal (H5034), to be foolish, to fade, to treat as worthless; kabad (H3513), to honour, literally to make weighty — the exact opposite.
roots_lines: Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, slight, of little weight; and so to make light of, to despise, to curse; 1 Samuel 2:30, Genesis 12:3.
Hebrew nabal (H5034) — to be senseless, to fade, to treat as worthless; Jeshurun lightly esteeming the Rock; Deuteronomy 32:15.
Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, and so to honour; honour and contempt in Scripture are a matter of assigned weight; 1 Samuel 2:30, Exodus 20:12.
usage: “Lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” — apostasy as a fall in weight, not a lost argument.
“Them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed” — exact reciprocity.
“I am a poor man, and lightly esteemed” — the anointed king's estimate of himself.

pos: adv. (particularly; above all; marking one item out of a class for special emphasis)
etymology: Latin specialis, particular, from species, a kind. In the Authorized Version specially and especially are used interchangeably, and both mark a narrower case inside a wider one.
biblical_def: Moses tells Israel to remember all the way, “specially the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb” (Deu 4:10) — one day out of forty years marked as the one never to be forgotten, when the mountain burned with fire and they heard the voice of words. Festus uses the word procedurally, bringing Paul out “specially before thee, O king Agrippa” (Act 25:26). Paul uses it twice in one letter, and both are weighty. First of God: “we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe” (1Ti 4:10). Second of the household: “if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8). In each case the structure is identical — a wide circle and a narrower one inside it, with the narrower named as the point of concentration. The whole nation had forty years of history; one day at Horeb was the day. God is the Saviour of all men in one sense; He is the Saviour of believers in another and fuller one. A man owes duty to many; he owes it first, and inescapably, at home.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines specially as particularly; in a manner beyond what is common; for a particular purpose; and chiefly, above all.
webster_full: SPECIALLY, adv. Particularly; in a manner beyond what is common.
2. For a particular purpose. A meeting of the legislature is specially summoned.
3. Chiefly; specially.
scriptures: Deu 4:10

Specially the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb, when the LORD said unto me, Gather me the people together, and I will make them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me all the days that they shall live upon the earth, and that they may teach their children.
For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 4:10 is the universalist's favourite verse, and the word specially is precisely what makes it useless for that purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: The living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe. Universalism reads the first clause and stops; if God is the Saviour of all men, all men are finally saved. But Paul wrote a second clause, and it is fatal to that reading, because specially distinguishes. If every man were saved in exactly the same sense, believers could not be marked out as a special case — there would be nothing to mark. The verse asserts two things at once, and the Reformed reading takes both. God is in a real sense the Saviour, the Preserver and Benefactor, of all men without exception: He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, gives rain and fruitful seasons, and in Him all men live and move and have their being. That is common grace, and Paul uses soter in the wide sense the Greek allows. And He is savingly, particularly, and effectually the Saviour of those that believe — which is definite atonement, and is the reason Paul labours and suffers reproach. Scripture nowhere teaches that all will be saved, and everywhere teaches that some will not: these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal. The same little word appears in the next chapter about a man's household, and it does the same work there: a Christian owes real duty to all men, and a nearer, sharper, non-negotiable duty to those under his own roof.
roots_summary: Greek malista (G3122), most of all, especially, chiefly; soter (G4990), saviour, preserver, benefactor; Hebrew emphatic particle marking the day at Horeb.
roots_lines: Greek malista (G3122) — most of all, chiefly, especially; the word that distinguishes believers within the wider circle and the household within the wider duty; 1 Timothy 4:10, 5:8.
Greek soter (G4990) — saviour, preserver, deliverer; used in the wide sense of God's common goodness and in the saving sense of Christ; 1 Timothy 4:10, Titus 2:13.
Hebrew yom (H3117) with the emphatic construction — “specially the day”; the day at Horeb singled out of forty years; Deuteronomy 4:10.
usage: “Specially the day that thou stoodest before the LORD thy God in Horeb” — one day out of forty years.
“The Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe” — and the second clause undoes the universalist reading.
“Specially for those of his own house” — the nearer duty, and a hard verdict on neglecting it.
